title: Learning Domain Trajectories with Flow Matching for Gradual Domain Adaptation
claim: Direct adaptation across a large distribution shift fails, but a path of intermediate domains makes the transfer gradual and feasible.
layout: Single panel; source left, target right, direct path crossed out above, curved path below
description: A single-panel cartoon on a white background. A blue cloud with dense blue dots on the left is labeled Source Domain D_s (Labeled). A red dot cluster on the right is labeled Target Domain D_t (Unlabeled). A dashed red arrow runs between them with a large red X over it, captioned 'Large Shift (Direct Adaptation Fails)'. Below, a solid green curved arrow labeled 'Proposed Gradual Shift Path' leaves the source, sags under three overlapping yellow-orange dotted clouds (Intermediate D_1, D_2 unlabeled in the middle, D_3), and rises to the target. Source and target labels are repeated near the lower ends of the path. The red X and the contrast between the dashed red and solid green arrows draw the eye first.
caption: Motivation of gradual domain adaptation under large distribution shifts. Gradual domain adaptation introduces intermediate domains to form a smooth transition path, reducing the discrepancy between consecutive domains and facilitating stable knowledge transfer.
abstract: Large distribution shifts remain a primary obstacle for domain generalization and unsupervised adaptation. Although gradual domain adaptation alleviates this difficulty by introducing ordered intermediate domains, most existing approaches still operate in a discrete, step-wise manner, which can accumulate errors and often relies on unstable Min--Max optimization. We propose \textbf{FlowGDA}, a flow-matching framework that models gradual adaptation as \emph{continuous} transport on a statistical manifold in a representation space. FlowGDA learns time-dependent velocity fields that induce smooth domain trajectories, using a simulation-free regression objective rather than adversarial training. To prevent semantic drift, we couple left-to-right transport between consecutive domains with a source-anchored transport and a semantic consistency loss, and we further stabilize learning via a two-stage sequential optimization scheme. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques, validating flow matching as an effective alternative for domain adaptation.
